title: Ideas I was right about: how Corey Haines mines his own idea folder for lessons
summary: Corey keeps a folder of hundreds of business ideas and reviews the ones others later built (HockeyStack, Navattic, SavvyCal, Fathom, TRMNL). He draws lessons about spotting pain points firsthand, ignoring "too hard to build" advice, and why he killed ideas that needed capital or two-sided marketplaces.

principles.text: Write down business ideas constantly; the habit trains you to spot opportunities worth pursuing.
principles.quote: Recording your business ideas trains your brain to think a certain way so that you can find ideas actually worth pursuing.

principles.text: Compare your ideas and assumptions to how others executed them to sharpen future judgment.
principles.quote: you can compare your ideas and assumptions to real-life application, and thus have better ideas and assumptions in the future.

principles.text: The best product ideas come from pain you feel yourself as a user of existing tools.
principles.quote: I did a lot of demos at Baremetrics, and Calendly drove me absolutely nuts.

principles.text: Let people try the product without signing up; public demos build trust and drive conversions.
principles.quote: I believed every product should be able to be demoed like this without having to sign up. And that the ones who did would earn more trust from their audience and have a competitive advantage.

principles.text: Don't let "too hard technically" naysaying kill an idea that customers clearly want.
principles.quote: Everyone I talked to said this would be too hard technically to build and that eventually everyone would want to bring it in house. I shouldn't have listened to them.

principles.text: Kill ideas whose economics are structurally heavy, like two-sided marketplaces without SEO or inventory-heavy rentals.
principles.quote: Ultimately I realized building a two sided marketplace that couldn't rely on SEO would take a massive amount of effort and time, so I killed it.
